title: The keepers of the gurdwaras
hookLine: hereditary keepers treated gurdwaras as private property

cards: A gurdwara door, and a man with the keys. He didn't build the gurdwara, and the sangat didn't choose him. He holds the keys because his teacher held them before him, and his teacher's teacher before that.
The offerings that pilgrims leave go into his keeping. The land around the shrine is written in his name. If the sangat doesn't like how he runs it, there isn't much they can do.

teach.b: A mahant is the head of a religious house, a title used beyond the Sikh tradition too.
Sikh histories say that in hard years, when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted and often far from home, gurdwaras were looked after by custodians, among them Udasis, an order of ascetics who honor Guru Nanak.

Thanks to them, doors stayed open. Over time the keeping passed from teacher to chosen disciple, or father to son. Under British rule the courts tended to treat the shrine and its land as the mahant's own property.

teach.h: A TRUST TURNS INTO AN ESTATE.
teach.b: What had been a trust began to look like an estate.
Some mahants, not all, lived well on the offerings and ran the gurdwaras as they pleased.
Reformers complained of practices in some shrines that they said went against the Gurus' teaching, and of a sangat with no say over its own house of worship.
Guru Nanak says that taking what rightly belongs to another is as forbidden as the food a person's own faith forbids.

teach.h: THE GURDWARA BELONGS TO THE SANGAT.
teach.b: A gurdwara belongs to the sangat.
When one man holds it as his own, something shared has slipped into private hands.

Looking back on this week: an exile dying in Paris, a princess marching, a princess keeping memory, soldiers far away, farmers on new land, Punjab arguing with itself, and now the keys of the gurdwaras in a few private hands.
A people without a kingdom, asking what was still theirs.

how: Sikh histories remember the era of the mahants as the background to the gurdwara reform movement, and they also honor the Udasi custodians who kept gurdwaras open in hard times.

games.q: you're in the sangat of a gurdwara. the mahant keeps the offerings and runs things as he pleases, and the land is in his name. what can you do, at this point in the story?
o: vote him out at the next meeting.
very little, because the law treats the shrine as his.
games.why: the courts tended to back the mahant's claim. changing that would take a long reform struggle, which comes later in the story.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that belongs to more than one person, a park, a shared kitchen, a family home, a community hall, a group's money, a tradition, and ask quietly who actually holds it: who has the keys, who makes the decisions, who cleans up?
Don't fix anything yet; just see it clearly. If you pray, say Waheguru as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Mahant. The head of a religious house; in Sikh history, a hereditary keeper of a gurdwara, some of whom came to treat the shrine as their own. Today's word.
